title: CORS policy decisions and misconfigurations
when: The user is about to open an API to other origins, or wants to fix a permissive CORS setup, and must decide whether CORS is needed and which origins and credentials to allow.
prompt:
Goal: The narrowest cross origin policy the clients need, written down, with the dangerous combinations ruled out.
Steps:
1. Ask if it is needed at all: one origin for page and API, or a dev proxy for /api, needs no CORS.
2. Keep the list per environment in config: CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com in production, http://localhost:5173 only in development.
3. Compare Origin by exact string equality; never startsWith, endsWith or an unanchored regex (example.com.evil.net and evilexample.com pass those).
4. Refuse the literal origin "null", which sandboxed frames and file pages send.
5. Cookies across origins need Allow-Credentials: true with one exact origin and a SameSite=None; Secure cookie; otherwise leave credentials off.
6. CORS only stops browsers from reading replies; the request still runs, so writes still need auth and CSRF checks.
Quality bar:
- Vary: Origin on every reply whose headers depend on Origin.
- The list is short and reviewed.
- README.md holds a table of origin, credentials and methods.
Pitfalls:
- Reflecting any Origin with credentials, letting any site read user data.
- Every origin allowed on an internal admin API.
- Believing a CORS error means the server never ran the request.
Verify:
- [ ] Origins match exactly.
- [ ] The null origin is refused.
- [ ] Credentials only with an exact origin.
- [ ] The policy table exists.
Output: Origin check updates in cors.mjs and a CORS section in README.md.

examples.input: nosso CORS devolve qualquer origin com credentials, esta certo?
examples.output: exact allowlist per environment, null refused, credentials only for app origin, Vary: Origin
